title: The Five Rules of the Workshop

post.author: u/night_apprentice_peronel
post.title: I'm the night apprentice at a furniture workshop. The cutting list for six walnut tabletops says 32 mm. The machine cut all six at 28. Both came from the same order.

blocks.text: I'm the night apprentice at Hartwick's, a workshop that makes furniture to measure. By day Mr Hartwick and two joiners build. By night I sweep, sharpen and mind the CNC router: a machine that carves wood by following numbers a computer sends it. CNC is short for computer numerical control. Over the bench Hartwick has painted his five rules. The first is *measure twice, cut once*.

The numbers come from a program Folarin wrote in Python, a programming language. In Python you describe a kind of thing once, as a class: a template that keeps a thing's facts together with the steps that act on them, like a recipe card with its ingredients. Folarin's program is one big class, Order, for one customer's job.
An order goes through five steps. First it prices the job at a rate per wood, plus a surcharge, an extra charge for dearer woods. Then it adds VAT, the sales tax.
Then it prints the cutting list: the sheet that gives each piece's size and thickness. Then it plans the oil finish. Last, at night, it sends each cut to the router.
Here is the class, shortened. Each step in a class is called a method, and each line starting *def* is one method. The words after # are Folarin's notes:

class Order:
  def price(self): ...         # rate per wood
  def surcharge(self): ...     # dear woods
  def add_vat(self): ...
  def cutting_list(self): ...  # thickness per wood
  def plan_finish(self): ...   # oil per wood
  def send_to_cnc(self):
    mm = {"oak": 28, "ash": 26}.get(self.wood, 28)
Five of the methods keep their own small table of woods, a lookup table, like a price list on a wall. The router's is the last line: oak 28 mm, ash 26 mm.
*.get* looks the wood up. If the wood isn't there, it uses the number after the comma: 28, oak's. That spare answer is called a fallback.
Last week Hartwick started selling walnut: 32 mm thick, with a 15 percent surcharge. Adding it meant editing five places: price, surcharge, cutting list, finish and router. Folarin edited four.

Order 2214 was six walnut tabletops for a restaurant. Its cutting list printed in the afternoon, and I clipped it to the stack of boards: 32 mm. At 01:00 the router started the night's three orders. Each line of its log shows the time, the order, the wood, the piece and the thickness it cut:

01:00  2212  oak     top 1 of 2  28 mm
01:24  2213  ash     top 1 of 3  26 mm
02:00  2214  walnut  top 1 of 6  28 mm
03:00  2214  walnut  top 6 of 6  28 mm
One order. Two records. Six tops that matched the wrong one.

At 06:00 I measured all six. 28 mm, every one, with the paper on top still saying 32. The router did exactly what it was told. Nobody told it about walnut, so it cut oak. You can take wood off a board. You can't put it back.

diagram.aria: Folarin's sketch of the Order class. Five methods sit in a column, each with its own table of woods. price, surcharge, cutting_list and plan_finish have walnut. send_to_cnc has no walnut and falls back to oak's 28 mm. cutting_list prints order 2214's cutting list at 32 mm; send_to_cnc sends the router 28 mm. Between them a note reads: one order, two thicknesses.

blocks.text: Folarin says programmers have five rules too, and that this class broke most of them. Hartwick wants a checklist. Cherry comes in spring. What should Folarin change before then?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Count the places in that class that know something about a wood. Each is a small table someone has to remember. When walnut came, what told each table? Nothing: Folarin had to find all five himself, and the program had no way to say one was missing. The 28 after the comma did its job, answering quietly instead of saying it didn't know. Now picture cherry. How many places will it have to reach? And who will tell the next table someone adds next year?

replies.author: u/night_apprentice_peronel
replies.text: Folarin counted again: five tables, the same woods in each, in a different order every time. Hartwick wants a checklist, a printed list of the five places, ticked off at every code review. That's when a second person reads a change to the code before it goes live.

comments.author: u/five_small_classes_melchior
comments.text: The real problem is that Order is too big. One class prices, taxes, cuts, oils and drives a machine; of course something got missed. Split it into five classes, one per job: Pricing, Tax, CuttingList, Finish, Router. Each one is small enough to read in a minute, with its own table right where it's used. Small classes don't hide mistakes. Split it and the problem goes away.

comments.author: u/fail_loud_dimitra
comments.text: Whatever else you do, get rid of that 28. Code that guesses is worse than code that stops. Make the router code refuse a wood it has no thickness for: it stops with an error message and wakes someone, instead of cutting six wrong tops. Stopping at the first sign of trouble is called failing fast.

replies.author: u/night_apprentice_peronel
replies.text: Folarin says that would have saved last night's walnut. He's less sure it saves the next wood.

reply.prompt: Cherry arrives in spring, and Folarin wants the program ready for it. What should he change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Make each wood a class holding its own thickness and surcharge, which every part asks for.
options.part2: Folarin wrote one base class, Wood, that lists what every wood must give: its thickness, its surcharge, its rate and its oil. Oak, Ash and Walnut each became a small class that fills those in, and every part of Order now asks the order's wood instead of keeping a table. The router line became *mm = self.wood.thickness_mm()*. Order 2214 was cut again at 32 mm. In March he added leg holes to the router, drilled from underneath. That cost four edits: one in Wood and one in each of the three woods. In spring cherry came: one new class, 22 mm, and nothing old touched. He left out the hole depth at first, and Python refused to make a Cherry until he gave one. On the night, order 2390's four cherry tops were cut at 22 mm and drilled 18 mm deep. The cutting list and the router agreed.
options.senior: Put each fact where it belongs: the wood knows its own thickness and surcharge, and everything else asks it. Adding a wood becomes adding one class, which is the open-closed idea: open to new woods, closed to edits in old code. The router depends on the idea of a Wood, not a list of names, and Python can insist every wood fills in every value. The price is paid the other way: a new kind of fact, like hole depth, now touches every wood class. Choose the shape by the kind of change you expect most.

options.text: Keep a checklist of the five places a new wood must be added, and check it in every review.
options.verdict: A list of places is not a design
options.part2: Hartwick pinned the five places above the router, and Folarin ticked them in every review. Walnut's router line was fixed, and order 2214 was cut again at 32 mm. In March Folarin added a sixth place, leg_holes(), which drills four holes for the legs from underneath. It had its own table and the same fallback, oak's 24 mm. Nobody added it to the list. In spring cherry came: six places to edit, five on the list, five ticks, all done. The router drilled 24 mm holes into 22 mm cherry. In the morning order 2390's four tops each had four small round holes in the polished face, 16 in all, coming up from a side nobody had touched.
options.senior: A checklist moves the knowledge out of the code and into people's memory, and memory is what failed. It works only while the list matches the code, and nothing checks the list. The code still has a place for every step that must hear about every wood. Change the shape so there is one place to edit, and keep checklists for what code can't check.

options.text: Make the CNC code refuse any wood it has no thickness for, instead of falling back to oak's.
options.verdict: Trade-off: stops the cut, keeps the spread
options.part2: Folarin took out the 28 and made send_to_cnc() stop with an error for any wood it has no thickness for. He tried it on a copy of walnut night: the router cut oak and ash, stopped at 02:00 on order 2214 and paged me. Six boards uncut, and safe. In March he added leg_holes(), which drills four holes for the legs from underneath, with its own table, copying the old pattern, fallback and all. In spring cherry needed six edits; he made five and missed the leg holes. The router knew cherry's thickness and cut 22 mm. Then it drilled oak's 24 mm holes. Order 2390's four tops came out with 16 holes through the face.
options.senior: Failing fast is a real improvement: a loud stop beats a quiet wrong answer, and it would have saved the walnut. But it guards one table, and only after the mistake is made. Every new wood still needs an edit in every place, and every new place needs its own guard. Keep the habit of failing fast, and also give each fact one home.

options.text: Split Order into five classes, one per job, each keeping its own table of woods and sizes.
options.part2: Folarin split Order into Pricing, Tax, CuttingList, Finish and Router, each small and tidy, each with its own table of woods. He tried it on a copy of walnut night: four classes had walnut, Router didn't, and the six tops came out at 28 mm again. In March leg holes became a sixth class, Drilling, which drills four holes for the legs from underneath, with a sixth table. In spring cherry needed six edits in six classes; Folarin made five. Order 2390's four tops were cut at 22 mm and drilled at oak's 24 mm: 16 holes through the face. Each class was easy to read. None of them knew what a wood was.
options.senior: One reason to change is a good rule, and the split follows it: Pricing changes when prices do. But the thing that varies here is the wood, and it is still copied into every class. Splitting by job without giving the wood a home spreads the same table over more files. Find what changes most often, and give that one home.

sim.title: Add a wood to Hartwick's program
sim.lede: You're Folarin, the night before order 2214 is cut. Three orders wait for the router at 01:00: 2212, two oak tops; 2213, three ash tops; 2214, six walnut tops. The router cuts one top every 12 minutes. Oak is 28 mm, ash 26 mm, walnut 32 mm, cherry 22 mm. In every design except a class per wood, each place in the code that knows about woods keeps its own table, and a missing wood falls back to oak's value. The same slip happens in every design: walnut misses the router's table; cherry misses leg_holes(), a sixth place added in March that drills four holes for the legs in each top, 4 mm short of its thickness. The checklist lists the five places as they were for walnut. With a class per wood, a wood that leaves a value out can't be made, so the program stops at start and the slip is fixed before the night. Pick a design and a new wood, then press Run the night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Run the night as built: order 2214 is cut at 28 mm against a 32 mm cutting list. Try the checklist, the refusing router, five classes and a class per wood, and run each. Then switch to cherry and watch the edits a new wood needs: 6, 6, 6, 6, then 1. Run cherry as built and count the leg holes through the top; then run it with a class per wood, and read what adding the sixth place cost.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the router was broken. The fact that walnut is 32 mm had to be copied into five tables; Folarin reached four, and the fifth answered with oak's number instead of saying it didn't know.

steps.title: Five tables, one fact, four copies.
steps.text: Adding walnut was a process of five edits, done by hand. First Folarin added it to price(), then to surcharge(), then to cutting_list(), then to plan_finish(). The fifth, send_to_cnc(), was missed, and nothing in the program could notice. At night the cutting list read walnut from its table and printed 32 mm. Then the router code looked walnut up in its own table, didn't find it, and took the fallback, 28. Two parts of one program answered the same question from two different tables, so one order got two records. What went wrong at each step was the same thing: the fact lived in five places, and every place had to be told.

steps.title: One reason to change, and Order had five.
steps.text: The first of the five rules, single responsibility, says a class should have one reason to change. Robert C. Martin says the reasons are people: whoever asks for the change. Order changes when Hartwick changes prices, when the tax changes, when the joiners change how they cut, when the finisher changes oils, and when the router changes. Every change risks the other four. But splitting by job alone, as u/five_small_classes_melchior suggested, keeps a table of woods in every class. The rule is about grouping what changes together, and here the wood is what changes.

steps.title: Open to new woods, closed to edits.
steps.text: The second rule, open-closed, says you should be able to add a new case by adding new code, not by changing code that already works. Give every wood its own class built on one base class, Wood, which names the values every wood must give. The router's process becomes three steps. First it asks the order for its wood. Then it asks that wood for its thickness. Then it cuts. Adding cherry is one new class, and no old line changes. What can go wrong: a new wood that leaves out a value. Python's abc module refuses to make an object from such a class, so the mistake stops the program at start, not the router at 02:00.

steps.title: Any wood must do: Liskov's rule.
steps.text: The third rule, Liskov substitution, says any subtype must work wherever its parent type is expected. Oak, Ash, Walnut and Cherry are subtypes of Wood, and the router only knows it has a Wood. That works only if every wood keeps the same promises: thickness_mm() means the whole board's thickness, in millimetres, and always gives an answer. A wood that gave inches, or raised an error, would break the router without breaking anything in its own class. Martin's point was that code that has to check which subtype it was given is code that must be edited for every new one.

steps.title: Small interfaces, and depending on an idea.
steps.text: The fourth rule, interface segregation, says keep what each user depends on small. The router needs a thickness, not a price or the tax, so give it the wood, not the whole order. The fifth, dependency inversion, says important code should depend on ideas, not details. send_to_cnc() depended on a detail: a word, "walnut", and its own table of words. With a Wood it depends on an idea, something that has a thickness, and works for woods nobody has thought of yet. All five are principles, not laws: they tell you where change will hurt, and you still choose.

diagram.aria: The fix. One base class, Wood, names what every wood must give: thickness_mm() and surcharge(). Order and the router both ask Wood. Below it, four wood classes fill those in: Oak 28 mm, Ash 26 mm, Walnut 32 mm with a 15 percent surcharge, and Cherry 22 mm, a new class. A note says cherry was one new class and no old code was edited.

nodes.label: Wood (base class)
nodes.meta: every wood must fill these in

notes.text: cherry: one new class, no old code edited

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for spring. Each wood is a class that knows its own thickness and surcharge, built on one base class, Wood. Order and the router both ask the order's wood, so there is no table to forget. Cherry arrived as one new class; nothing above it was edited.

fix.title: The fix: each wood a class that knows its own facts, and every part asks it
fix.text: Write one base class, Wood, whose abstract methods name everything a wood must give: thickness, surcharge, rate and oil. Make Oak, Ash and Walnut small classes that fill those in. Change every part of Order, and the router code, to ask the order's wood instead of keeping a table: mm = self.wood.thickness_mm(). Delete the five tables and the fallback to 28. Hand the router the wood, not the whole order. Adding cherry is then one new class; if it leaves a value out, Python refuses to make it and the program stops at start. Re-cut order 2214 at 32 mm.

limits: It makes new woods cheap and new kinds of fact dear. When Folarin added leg holes in March, that was four edits: one in Wood and one in each of the three woods. If the workshop adds new steps more often than new woods, a table per step may be the better shape.
The base class checks that every value exists, not that it's right. A Cherry class that says 32 mm will be cut at 32 mm. Each new wood still needs one careful check against the supplier's sheet.
These are principles, not laws. A program with two woods that never change doesn't need a class for each; apply them where change actually comes, and stop where it doesn't.

head: Design
Good
Bad
rows: Everything in one file. Easy to start with.
A new wood means five edits; a missed one falls back to oak's numbers in silence.
As built, plus a checklist in review
Catches a missed place that's on the list. No code changes.
Only as good as the list. A sixth place that nobody adds to it is missed.
As built, router refuses unknown woods
A loud stop instead of a wrong cut. Cheap to add tonight.
Guards one table, after the mistake. Every new wood still needs every edit.
Each class is small and has one job.
Five tables of woods instead of one class with five. The same five edits.
A class per wood, which every part asks
A new wood is one new class. A missing value stops the program at start.
A new kind of fact touches every wood class. More classes to read.

explain.seniorTake: The five rules are questions about where change will land, not a score to give code. Find the thing that varies, here the wood, and give it one home that every other part asks. Then a new case is new code, old code stays still, and a missing fact stops the program at start instead of the router at 02:00. Keep classes small for the right reason: one reason to change each, not one method each. Keep the habit of failing fast too: a program that says it doesn't know beats one that guesses. And know the cost: the shape that makes one kind of change cheap makes the other kind dearer.

realWorld.title: Robert C. Martin: the five, in his own words
realWorld.text: In 2020 Martin summed the principles up. Single responsibility: "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons. Separate things that change for different reasons." Open-closed: "A Module should be open for extension but closed for modification." Liskov substitution: "A program that uses an interface must not be confused by an implementation of that interface." Interface segregation: "Keep interfaces small so that users don't end up depending on things they don't need." Dependency inversion: "Depend in the direction of abstraction. High level modules should not depend upon low level details."

realWorld.title: One reason to change, and the reasons are people
realWorld.text: In 2014 Martin wrote that the Single Responsibility Principle "states that each software module should have one and only one reason to change", and that "the reasons for change are people. It is people who request changes." At Hartwick's those people are the owner, the tax office, the joiners, the finisher and the router.

realWorld.title: Open-closed, in 1996
realWorld.text: In his C++ Report column of 1996, Martin described the open-closed principle as saying "that in a well designed program new features are added by adding new code, rather than by changing old, already working, code."

realWorld.title: Barbara Liskov's substitution property
realWorld.text: Martin quotes Liskov's 1988 paper Data Abstraction and Hierarchy: "What is wanted here is something like the following substitution property: If for each object o1 of type S there is an object o2 of type T such that for all programs P defined in terms of T, the behavior of P is unchanged when o1 is substituted for o2 then S is a subtype of T."

realWorld.title: Why breaking it breaks open-closed
realWorld.text: In the same column Martin wrote that a function that doesn't conform to the substitution principle "must know about all the derivatives of that base class", and that "Such a function violates the Open-Closed principle because it must be modified whenever a new derivative of the base class is created."

realWorld.title: Python can insist every wood fills in every value
realWorld.text: Python's abc module "provides the infrastructure for defining abstract base classes (ABCs) in Python". Its documentation says "A class that has a metaclass derived from ABCMeta cannot be instantiated unless all of its abstract methods and properties are overridden." That is what turns a forgotten thickness into a stop at start.

asked: Show me a class that breaks single responsibility.
How would you add a new type without editing old code?
interview.answer: SOLID is five design principles gathered by Robert C. Martin. Single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change, meaning one group of people whose requests change it. Open-closed: you add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing code that works. Liskov substitution: any subtype must work wherever its parent is expected, keeping the parent's promises. Interface segregation: keep what each caller depends on small. Dependency inversion: important code depends on abstractions, not on details. For a class that breaks single responsibility, I'd describe an Order class that prices, adds tax, writes a cutting list and drives a machine: it changes when prices, tax law, the workshop or the machine change, and each change risks the others. To add a new type without editing old code, find what varies, say the material or the payment method, and make it a small class behind one shared interface, with the facts and behaviour that belong to it. Callers ask the object instead of switching on its name, so a new type is one new class. In Python I'd make the interface an abstract base class, so a new type that misses a method can't even be created. I'd also say what it costs: a new kind of operation now touches every type, and these are principles to weigh, not laws.

terms.def: A trainee who works the night shift. Peronel sweeps, sharpens tools and minds the router at Hartwick's while the joiners are home.
A woodworker who cuts and fits pieces of wood together to make furniture.
A machine that carves and cuts wood by following numbers a computer sends it: where to move and how deep to cut. Like a very steady hand that reads instructions.
Short for computer numerical control: a machine tool driven by numbers from a computer instead of by hand.
A list of instructions a computer follows. Hartwick's program prices each order and sends its cuts to the router.
A programming language: a way of writing instructions for a computer that people can read. Folarin wrote Hartwick's program in it.
A template in code for one kind of thing, keeping its facts together with the steps that act on them, like a recipe card with its ingredients. Order is a class.
One thing made from a class, with its own facts. Order 2214 is one Order object; one walnut board would be one Walnut object.
One step a class can do, written as a small block of code that starts with def in Python. price() and send_to_cnc() are methods of Order.
One customer's job at Hartwick's, and the class in Folarin's program that holds it: the wood, the pieces and the price.
An extra charge on top of the normal price. Walnut carries a 15 percent surcharge because the timber costs more.
Short for value added tax: a sales tax added to the price of most goods and services.
A sheet that lists every piece to cut for an order, with its size and thickness. The joiners and the router are meant to follow the same one.
The oil or wax put on wood at the end to protect it. Each wood gets its own.
A list of names, each with its answer, that code looks things up in, like a price list on a wall. send_to_cnc() has one: oak 28 mm, ash 26 mm.
A Python step that looks a name up in a table. If the name isn't there, it gives back the spare answer written after the comma instead of an error.
A spare answer code uses when it can't find the real one. send_to_cnc() falls back to oak's 28 mm for any wood it doesn't know.
A second person reading a change to the code before it goes live, looking for mistakes.
A printed list of steps to tick off. Hartwick's would list the five places in the code a new wood must be added to.
A message a program gives when it can't go on, stopping that piece of work instead of guessing.
Stopping with a clear error at the first sign something is wrong, instead of guessing and carrying on. A router that refuses an unknown wood fails fast.
Send an urgent alert to a person's phone so they wake up and look.
Holes drilled into the underside of a tabletop where the legs fit. They must stop short of the face, or they come through the top.
A class that lists what a family of classes must provide. Wood is one: every wood must give its thickness, surcharge, rate and oil.
A class built on a base class that fills in its details. Oak, Ash and Walnut are subclasses of Wood.
A type is a kind of value or object, such as a number or a Wood. A subtype is a narrower kind meant to stand in for it: Walnut is a subtype of Wood.
A method a base class names but leaves empty. In Python, a subclass that doesn't fill in every abstract method can't be made at all.
Python's built-in tools for abstract base classes. It refuses to make an object from a class that leaves an abstract method empty.
What a piece of code promises to offer others, without saying how. The router needs only one thing from a wood: its thickness.
An idea that hides the details. Wood stands for any wood, so code that asks a Wood for its thickness works for woods not yet added.
Five design principles gathered by Robert C. Martin, named from their first letters: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
A class should have one reason to change: one group of people whose requests change it. Order had five.
Code should be open to new cases and closed to edits: a new wood is added as new code, without changing code that already works.
Any subtype must work wherever its parent type is expected, keeping the parent's promises. Named after Barbara Liskov.
Keep what each user of a class depends on small, so nothing depends on things it doesn't need. The router needs a thickness, not a price.
Important code should depend on ideas, not details: the router asks a Wood for its thickness instead of looking a word up in its own table.
A software engineer and author who wrote about these design principles from the 1990s on and gathered them as SOLID.
A computer scientist. Her 1988 paper Data Abstraction and Hierarchy described when one type can safely stand in for another; the substitution principle is named after her.
A piece of a program kept together in its own file or class. Martin uses it for any part you might change on its own.
The code that actually does what an interface promises. Each wood class is one implementation of Wood.
An older word for a subclass: a class built on another one. Martin's 1996 column uses it.
A thin skin of good wood glued over a cheaper board, so the board looks like solid wood.

atWork: Look for a decision on a type's name that is repeated in more than one file: an if-else or switch on the payment method, the region, the shipping company or the plan. A common pattern: adding one more payment method meant editing the same switch in fees, refunds, receipts and fraud checks, and the one that was missed quietly took the default branch. Read-only access is enough to check. Search the code for the name of one existing type and count the files it appears in; each is a place a new type must reach. Then look at each switch's default branch: does it stop with an error, or quietly pick one of the others? If the count is more than two or three and new types arrive often, that type wants to be a small class behind one shared interface, so the next one is a new class instead of a hunt through the code. If new types are rare and new operations are common, the switch may be the better shape; say so in the review.

recall.prompt: Your shop's checkout code decides how to take each payment with an if-else on the payment method's name, and the same if-else is repeated in seven files: fees, refunds, receipts, fraud checks and more. Adding a new payment method last month meant seven edits. One was missed, and refunds for the new method quietly went down the card branch. What would you change, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: Knowledge of each payment method is spread over many places, so every new method means editing them all, and one gets missed
Make each payment method a class that knows its own behaviour, so adding a method is one new class
Callers depend on one shared interface, not the method's name, and a missing piece fails at start (an abstract method) instead of falling back quietly

recall.model: The knowledge of what each payment method does is spread over seven files, so every new method means seven edits, and one will sooner or later be missed; the default branch then hides the miss. Make each payment method its own class behind one shared interface, with methods for fees, refunds, receipts and fraud checks, and have the checkout code ask the payment object instead of testing its name. Adding a method is then one new class. Make the interface an abstract base class so a new method that leaves out, say, refunds can't be created, and remove the default branch, so a missing piece fails fast at start instead of quietly going down the card path.

recall.prompt: At Hartwick's, send_to_cnc() looked walnut up in its own table and, finding nothing, used oak's 28 mm. Which change would have made adding walnut a single edit in one place?
options: A printed checklist of the five places, ticked in every review
A router that stops with an error on any wood it doesn't know
Five classes, one per job, each keeping its own table of woods
One class per wood, holding its own facts, which every part asks
recall.why: The checklist, the refusing router and the five classes all keep a table of woods in every place, so a new wood still means five edits. A class per wood puts walnut's thickness and surcharge in one place; the router and Order ask the wood, so adding walnut is one new class.

recall.prompt: A teammate's ReportJob class fetches sales from the database, works out the totals, lays them out as a PDF and emails it to the managers. Last week the finance team changed how refunds are counted, and the edit broke the PDF's page layout. What rule does this class break, and how would you change it without overdoing it?

keyIdeas.idea: It has several reasons to change, each coming from a different group of people
Split it by reason: fetching, totals, layout and sending in separate pieces that a small job connects
Stop at one piece per reason to change, not one class per method; a principle, not a law

recall.model: It breaks single responsibility: the class has four reasons to change, coming from different people. Finance owns how totals are counted, the managers own how the report looks, and whoever runs the database and the mail owns fetching and sending. Because they share one class, a finance change broke the layout. Split it into separate classes by reason: one fetches sales, one works out the totals, one lays out the PDF, one sends the email, and a small ReportJob connects them. Don't go too far: the aim is one piece per reason to change, not one class per method, and it's a principle to weigh, not a law.

recall.prompt: Folarin's first draft of the new router code was given the whole Order, so it could read prices and tax as well as the wood. Which of the five rules says it should be handed only what it needs?
recall.why: Interface segregation says keep what each user depends on small. The router needs a thickness, not prices or tax; handed the whole order, it depends on things it never uses, and a change to pricing can reach it. Hand it the wood. Dependency inversion is about depending on an idea rather than a detail, open-closed about adding new cases without edits, and single responsibility about how many reasons a class has to change.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The wood classes have held. Cherry was one class and nothing old was touched. Last week Folarin added WalnutVeneer, a cheaper board: an 18 mm plain core with a 0.6 mm skin of walnut glued on each face. He wrote its thickness_mm() to give 0.6, because that's how thick the walnut is. Overnight the router took order 2671, eight veneered shelves. In the morning each board had a faint groove traced around the shape, as if someone had run a fingernail round it, and not one shelf was cut out.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the router only scratch the boards, and what should Folarin change?

keyIdeas.idea: WalnutVeneer broke the promise every Wood makes, that thickness_mm() is the whole board, so it can't safely stand in for a Wood: Liskov substitution
Give the board's full thickness from thickness_mm() and keep the veneer's thickness as a separate value
Check the promise in one place: one test that runs every Wood subclass through the same checks

coldCase.model: The router trusted the promise every Wood makes: thickness_mm() is the whole board, in millimetres. WalnutVeneer kept the method's name but changed its meaning, so it couldn't stand in for a Wood. That is the Liskov substitution rule broken: the router did nothing wrong, it cut 0.6 mm deep through a board that is 19.2 mm. Make thickness_mm() give the full board, core plus both skins, and put the walnut skin in a separate value, a new method such as veneer_mm(), for whoever needs it. Then add one test that runs every subclass of Wood through the same checks, such as a board thickness between 10 and 60 mm, so the next wood that bends the promise fails the test instead of the shelves.
